vignette: Rukmini had always been a woman of precision and control. As an airline pilot for over four decades, she was known for her calm demeanor and exceptional flying skills. But behind closed doors, Rukmini's life had been forever changed by the traumatic events of her childhood. Growing up in a traditional South Asian household, Rukmini witnessed the brutal domestic violence inflicted upon her mother by her father. The memories of those nights, with their sound of shattering glass and her mother's muffled cries, still lingered vividly in her mind. As she lay in bed, Rukmini would often relive the event, feeling as though it was happening all over again - the same fear, the same helplessness. As an adult, Rukmini developed strategies to cope with the lingering distress. She began to overeat, using food as a way to comfort herself when memories of her childhood resurfaced. But this coping mechanism only led to feelings of guilt and shame, reinforcing her negative self-appraisal that she was a "lousy coper." At night, Rukmini would stay awake until the early hours, delaying sleep in an attempt to avoid the nightmares that inevitably followed. Certain triggers still had the power to transport Rukmini back to those childhood nights. The smell of hospitals or antiseptic, reminiscent of her mother's frequent trips to the emergency room, could send her into a tailspin of anxiety. Even certain songs, played during particularly tumultuous periods in her life, could evoke the same feelings of dread and fear. Rukmini's irritability had become a concern for those closest to her. Her husband, with whom she had been married for over 50 years, would often find himself on the receiving end of her anger outbursts, which left him bewildered and worried. At home, Rukmini felt perpetually "on guard," as though danger was lurking around every corner. Sleeping alone or in unfamiliar places was particularly challenging for Rukmini. Without the comforting presence of her husband, she would wake up multiple times during the night to check whether she was safe. Her memories of the traumatic event remained fragmented and disconnected, making it difficult for her to piece together a coherent narrative. As time went on, Rukmini's avoidance behaviors began to take a toll on her daily life. She had to stop flying long-haul flights due to chronic fatigue and stress-related health issues. Her relationships with loved ones became strained as she increasingly withdrew from social interactions. The recent loss of a close friend, who had also been a victim of domestic violence, sent Rukmini into a downward spiral of grief and self-doubt. It was this event that finally prompted her to seek help, as she realized that she could no longer rely on herself to manage the distress that had been simmering beneath the surface for so long. Now, at 79 years old, Rukmini is seeking therapy with a mix of trepidation and hope. She fears confronting the memories she has tried to keep buried for so long but hopes to finally find a way to break free from the grip of her traumatic past. As she sits in the therapist's office, fidgeting with her hands, Rukmini whispers, "I'm not sure I can do this, but I know I have to try."
